# Results — Study 357 (the Coffee-Can portfolio)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Robert Kirby's "buy quality names
and never sell" portfolio, tested on a real monthly total-return tape and a deterministic
survivorship control. We run a zero-turnover buy-and-hold of a quality large-cap basket against
a yearly-rebalanced twin (charged costs) and against the index (SPY), then quantify the
survivorship inflation directly. Offline core is deterministic (seed 357); run
`python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance monthly **total-return** closes (`auto_adjust=True`: splits + dividends), public Yahoo endpoint, no key |
| Window | 2005-01 → 2026-05 (**256** monthly returns; **21.3** years) |
| Basket | KO · JNJ · PG · PEP · WMT · MMM · MO · XOM · IBM · GE (equal-weight; a *survivorship sample* of still-famous large-caps) |
| Benchmark | SPY (S&P 500 total return) |
| Synthetic control | 400-firm panel, identical 8%/yr drift, 22% vol, 3%/yr death hazard, seed 357 (offline, deterministic) |
| As-of | 2026-06-22 (the in-progress 2026-06 month is excluded; last return is 2026-05) |

> **Scope caveats (named on the axes).** *Signal* — the basket is itself chosen with hindsight,
> so even its real-tape numbers are an **upper bound**; the survivorship control measures how
> large that inflation can be. *Tradability* — one 21-year regime, one large-cap basket; the
> cost tailwind is regime-dependent (it grows with turnover and tax).

## Half 1 — no RETURN edge over the index (the can does not beat the market)

Buy-and-hold the basket (weights drift, never trade) vs the index. The Signal-axis statistic is
the paired *t* of the can's monthly **excess** over SPY, with a Newey-West (HAC, lag 6) SE.

| portfolio | CAGR | vol | Sharpe | max drawdown |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Coffee Can (zero turnover) | **9.49%** | 12.58% | 0.786 | **−30.6%** |
| Rebalanced yearly (net 10bps) | 10.28% | 12.76% | 0.834 | −31.9% |
| **S&P 500 (index)** | **11.11%** | 15.13% | 0.775 | −50.8% |

| comparison | mean excess (ann.) | t (iid) | t (HAC-6) | p (HAC-6) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| can − index | **−1.84%** | −0.81 | **−0.83** | 0.41 |
| can − rebalanced twin | −0.75% | — | −1.26 | 0.21 |

The can **underperformed** the index on return (−1.84%/yr, HAC *t* = −0.83 — insignificant and
the *wrong* sign), and even trailed its own rebalanced twin. **H₁ (return edge) is rejected.**

## Half 2 — a real RISK edge (the can is calmer, not richer)

Where the can delivers: it gave up ~1.6 pp/yr of return to buy **2.5 pp** lower volatility and a
drawdown **20 pp** shallower (−30.6% vs the index's −50.8% in 2008). On a risk-adjusted basis it
**ties** the index (Sharpe 0.786 vs 0.775). This is a defensive, low-beta, staples-heavy tilt —
*de-risking*, not alpha. Hence the Signal stamp is **MIXED** (None on return · Real on risk),
not REAL.

## Half 3 — the cost tailwind is real but tiny (the honest part)

CAGR of the yearly-rebalanced twin as the one-way trading cost rises. The never-trade can pays
its cost **once** (≈ 0.10% of NAV at entry, at 10bps) and never again.

| one-way cost / rebalance | rebalanced CAGR |
|---|--:|
| 0 bps | 10.296% |
| 10 bps | 10.284% |
| 20 bps | 10.272% |

The cost wedge at a **yearly** rebalance is ~**1 bp/yr** (third-decimal). Costs only "feast" on
a high-churn active fund or a taxable account realising gains constantly — i.e. the *active
manager* the legend beats, **not** the index. The low-cost benefit is real and defensible, but
immaterial against the index.

## Half 4 — survivorship inflates the apparent edge (the catch, measured)

A deterministic 400-firm panel where **every firm has the same true 8%/yr drift** — there is
*no* cross-sectional skill to find — and a 3%/yr death hazard (delist → 95% wipe; **189 of 400
firms, 47%, are dead by the end**). Build the can three ways:

| basket (same universe) | CAGR | what it is |
|---|--:|---|
| famous names (top *terminal* value — **look-ahead**) | **17.08%** | the coffee-can selection bias |
| honest names (top *early* return — **ex-ante**) | 8.92% | the honest counterfactual |
| whole universe (EW, deaths included) | 4.72% | the actual truth (~8% drift, dragged by deaths) |

**Survivorship gap = +8.16 pp/yr** (famous vs honest) / **+12.36 pp/yr** (famous vs the
death-inclusive universe) — *entirely fake*, since every firm shares the same drift. A no-death
control returns **8.23% ≈ 8%** for the whole universe (confirming the engine is unbiased), with
the residual famous-lift being pure look-ahead order-statistics. **H₃ (no survivorship) is
decisively false.**

## Verdict

- **Signal — MIXED.** Return excess over SPY = −1.84%/yr (HAC *t* = −0.83, n = 256): **no**
  return edge, wrong sign. But a genuine **risk** edge — MDD −30.6% vs −50.8%, Sharpe 0.786 vs
  0.775. *None on return · Real on risk.* And even that real-tape result is survivorship-inflated
  (the basket is famous names).
- **Tradability — FRAGILE.** The honest cost tailwind is ~1 bp/yr at a yearly rebalance, and the
  can trails its own rebalanced twin. The low-cost/low-tax benefit is real but immaterial against
  the index; the headline out-performance needs hindsight.
- **Survivorship? — CONFIRMED.** On a no-skill panel, look-ahead selection manufactures +8.16
  pp/yr (vs honest) / +12.36 pp/yr (vs the death-inclusive universe). The legend's "magic" is
  mostly choosing winners after the fact.

> The discipline (low cost, low stress, defensive tilt) is real and worth having. The
> *out-performance* is mostly survivorship — buy the calm, not the legend.
